newsitem.title: USA: Disney shareholders approve Eisner's contract.
newsitem.headline: Disney shareholders approve Eisner's contract.

text.p: Walt Disney Co. shareholders approved a new contract Tuesday for Chairman Michael Eisner despite a hailstorm of opposition from critics who called the compensation package excessive.

In a rancorous meeting that lasted more than four hours at the home of Disney's Mighty Ducks professional hockey team here, executives tried repeatedly to project an upbeat outlook using fireworks, singers and even a brief satellite discussion with ABC News anchor Peter Jennings to underscore Disney's global reach.

The presentation failed, however, to sway many shareholders who demanded to know why Disney chose to give former president Michael Ovitz millions of dollars in severance pay and reward Eisner with a new 10-year contract that critics claim could be worth as much as $400 million.
"I have nothing against Mr. Eisner," said one shareholder. "He's done a fine job, but I think (this contract) is a little too lucrative."
"He's paid more than the president of the United States," added another shareholder.
Eisner acknowledged the decision to hire Ovitz was "a mistake in judgment" but he said once he realised he had made an error he moved quickly to fix it.
"The cost to the company, as high as it was, would have been much higher if we had stayed the unstayable course," Eisner said.

Ovitz, who headed up Hollywood's powerful Creative Artists Agency, was hired to help run Disney after it acquired Capital Cities/ABC Inc. last year. He quickly clashed with other Disney executives and decided to step down after only 14 months on the job.
Time and again Disney officials were greeted with boos and shouts from the audience as they tried to explain the terms of Ovitz' contract and the details of Eisner's contract.

But, in the end, more than 88 percent of the votes cast at the meeting were in favour of Eisner's new contract. Shareholders also approved a new cash bonus performance plan for top executive officers and supported the re-election of five current board members. However, more than 12.5 percent of shares were voted to withhold support for the board, a higher-than-usual percentage.

Disney's board of directors has come under fire for the decision to pay Ovitz nearly $39 million in cash and stock options on 3 million shares currently worth about $56 million. Some investors, including the influential California Public Employees' Retirement System, voted against the nominees, claiming the board has become a rubber stamp for Eisner.

Eisner, who took the unusual step of defending the board during lengthy introductory comments, responded to the critics, saying many board members helped keep Disney intact when it was the subject of takeover attempts in 1984.
"This is an active board," Eisner said. "One that is supportive but also demanding."

Since the arrival of Eisner and the late Frank Wells in 1984, Eisner said Disney's fortunes have improved dramatically with annual revenues soaring to nearly $19 billion from $1.5 billion. He said a $1,000 investment in Disney in 1984 would be worth $22,274.09 today, a growth rate of 2,445 percent.

While some shareholders praised Eisner's efforts, at least two shareholders said Disney should deduct from Eisner's compensation package the amount of the settlement to Ovitz in light of Eisner's admission that he made a mistake when he hired him.
"To recognise a mistake is one thing but to reward a mistake is another," one shareholder said. "This isn't a one-man company. He is not the only one responsible for the overall success."

Under terms of Eisner's new contract his base salary remains unchanged at $750,000 but he also is entitled to receive options for 8 million Disney shares which the company estimates are worth about $195 million. He is also eligible to receive millions of dollars in bonuses if the company's stock rises.
Raymond Watson, a member of the company's board of directors and chairman of its executive committee, defended the contract, saying much of the pay depends on how well Disney does.
"We are not shy about the fact that we have awarded him a contract that says if you are successful ... you will be rewarded," Watson told the audience.
